articles.title_orig: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China | US foreign policy
articles.title_zh: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China | US foreign policy
articles.content_orig:
When Xi Jinping, China’s leader, touches down in Maryland on Wednesday, he will step out into the arms – perhaps a hug, if Donald Trump’s wishes come true – of a US president who has shown China more bonhomie than any of his recent predecessors.
The meeting between Xi and Trump this week will be the second time that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. At the previous summit, held in Beijing in May, there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers. But there was little by way of concrete outcomes: the countries remain at loggerheads over trade, export controls and geopolitics.
Despite the goodwill built in May, few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week when Xi makes his first state visit to the US since 2015. “Expectations are very low,” said Bonnie Glaser, a managing director at the US thinkthank the German Marshall Fund. “Nobody is using the term ‘deliverables’.”
One area in which Trump and Xi may reach some consensus is on artificial intelligence safety. Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening.
In the past few weeks, the US has been beset by worries that AI is progressing too fast, but that the US must strive to defend its lead over China in the frontier technology – and Trump has pushed back hard against calls to slow its development. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said recently. “And frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”
On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, concluded talks with the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng by proposing an AI safety mechanism to be established between Washington and Beijing. The mechanism appears to stop short of a major safety agreement.
Tuesday’s front page of the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist party (CCP), ran an article saying that the US and China should “make AI a new frontier for China-US cooperation” and “make good use of the intergovernmental dialogue mechanism on AI”.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, called on the two countries to establish a dialogue on AI similar to the communication between the US and the Soviet Union during the cold war. “Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said.
Still, China does not agree with US assessments about the grave threat posed by its AI developments. China’s foreign ministry responded to an essay by Dario Amodei, the Anthropic chief executive, which called for Washington to impede Beijing’s progress by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
China has already taken steps to mandate the labelling of AI-generated content, to restrict the ability of children to use AI companions and, in keeping with the CCP’s desire to keep tight control on all information, to restrict what can be said by chatbots.
China may be more concerned with what it sees as US attempts to limit is growth. Washington has for years restricted China’s ability to buy the most advanced semiconductors needed for AI development, and this year the US banned the sale of Chinese humanoid robots.
Amanda Hsiao, China director at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy, said: “China doesn’t necessarily see the threat in the same way that the US does. There is a lot of distrust that’s in the way of cooperation. The Chinese are inclined to think of every US call for safety standards or calls from companies for pacing the frontier as means of suppressing Chinese development.”
Next on the agenda will be trade. Washington and Beijing struck a temporary truce in the trade war last year at a summit in South Korea. That truce – which included a pause on tariffs, as well as an agreement for Beijing to loosen restrictions on the export of rare earths – will expire in November.
Beijing is hoping for a longer-term commitment to banish tariffs, which pose a threat to China’s export-driven economy. But reports suggest that the US is unwilling to agree to anything that would weaken its future bargaining power.
Glaser, of the German Marshall Fund, said: “The US side views this as leverage over China and ensuring that they can get deliveries of the rare earths and magnets that American companies need.”
China may not feel the need to negotiate, either. Despite the trade war, China’s exports have surged, and it is on track to reach a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running.
One aspect of the relationship that has shifted since May is the issue of Taiwan. After the Beijing summit, Xi secured a major concession from Trump, when he agreed to pause a $14bn package of US arms sales to Taiwan. US presidents have traditionally excluded the issue of arms sales to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, from the US-China relationship.
But Trump has described future weapons sales as a “very good negotiating chip”. The US is now reportedly considering delaying further sales until after the Apec and G20 summits later this year, where Trump and Xi are expected to meet again.
Tuesday’s People’s Daily article said that a stable China-US relationship would “bring more peace, prosperity, and progress to the world”. But for all the talk in Beijing of “strategic stability”, Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, notes that “this is not a G2” alliance of the world’s two dominant powers.
“They are finding a way to manage the bilateral relationship, but they are not whatsoever working together as co-stewards of the international order,” Kennedy wrote in a recent commentary.
China is Iran’s biggest oil buyer and trading partner. After Trump launched strikes against Iran in February, China reportedly put pressure on Tehran behind the scenes to come to the negotiating table. It also slashed oil imports by nearly one-quarter in the first six months of the war, limiting global inflation.
Da Wei, a professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, wrote in a recent essay that this reflected “a more confident China” that “did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran”. But Beijing has otherwise done little to resolve the crisis in the Middle East, which it sees as being a mess of Trump’s making.
Last month, Bessent announced an “economic D-day” against Iran and its enablers. The US treasury secretary subsequently claimed to have had “very good private discussions” with Chinese officials over ending the country’s economic ties with Iran.
When it comes to Ukraine, Beijing has shown unwavering support for Moscow since Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, launched his full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser on the US and China at the International Crisis Group, said: “The contrast between the world’s incumbent power and its principal challenger will be even sharper in Washington than it was in Beijing in May: while the former is mired once more in the Middle East and straining longstanding alliances, the latter is casting itself as a stabilizing counterweight and the leading champion of a more multipolar order.”
The lack of momentum on thorny geopolitical issues, combined with China’s emphasis on maintaining “strategic stability” above all else, means that few expect there to be major breakthroughs at this week’s summit.
Hsiao added: “It is going to be yet another summit that is high on positive vibes and relatively low ambition in terms of substance.”

articles.title_orig: China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents - International Consortium of Investigative Journalists
articles.title_zh: China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents - International Consortium of Investigative Journalists
articles.content_orig:
China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents
ICIJ’s media partners uncovered strategic deals and moves the Chinese bank made around the world to further the political priorities of the party-state.
China Capital, an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists in collaboration with 23 media partners, provided an unprecedented look into decision-making at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, one of the most powerful Chinese institutions, at a time of China’s ascendance on the world stage.
The investigation is based on more than 4.8 million confidential records from two of ICBC’s U.K. units. The records provide rare insight into one of China’s most important financial arms, showing how the government’s influence and political priorities often outweigh ordinary banking protocols.
This is the first time that an international team of reporters has examined the inner workings and lending practices of ICBC– the world’s largest bank by asset size. Like many of its state-owned peers, ICBC is notoriously secretive.
“The ICIJ investigation shows how branch structures can be leveraged by foreign bank headquarters to override local compliance officers when state-backed corporate interests conflict with local regulatory obligations,” said David P. Weber, an accounting professor at West Virginia University and former Chief Investigator of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. He urged regulators in the U.S. and the U.K. to implement a cross-border enforcement mechanism that could “reduce oversight fragmentation.”
From New Zealand to Mexico, the 75 journalists who participated in the investigation uncovered previously unknown details about the bank’s involvement in some of their countries’ most important infrastructure projects and natural resources companies, as well as deals with firms linked to China’s military apparatus. Here are some of the revelations they uncovered.
The bank did not respond to reporters’ requests for comment.
How ICBC blended commercial interests with China’s political priorities
ICIJ’s partners across India, New Zealand and Austria found repeated instances where the bank’s political role blended with its commercial interests.
In 2017, Indian and Chinese troops reached a stand-off in the disputed Doklam region at the two countries’ borders, after the Indian government accused Beijing-backed companies of building roads in a territory claimed by China and Bhutan, in violation of a 1980 treaty. The two-month face-off didn’t just have political repercussions, The Indian Express, an ICIJ partner, reported. It also triggered actions inside ICBC’s Mumbai branch, more than 1,200 miles south of the border.
Soon after the news reached the bankers, ICBC “suspended the disbursement of 11 approved but undisbursed loans and bond investments totalling $185 million,” according to internal records. The bank also “organized” Chinese Communist Party members across every department to stay in constant touch with China’s embassy and consulate. The incident exemplifies the bank’s tight links to the party-state and how geopolitical events can influence its lending operations around the world.
Like most Chinese companies, ICBC has a Communist Party committee, an internal cell that ensures its operations advance the party’s interests, and some bankers were internally referred to as “comrades.”
In New Zealand, The Post reported that a Communist Party member who worked as a senior executive at ICBC’s Auckland outpost handled the local accounts of Hikvision, a Chinese surveillance tech company with links to the government. Numerous investigations by researchers and journalists have documented how, since at least 2017, Hikvision has provided surveillance technology to forces in Xinjiang, the Chinese region where Xi Jinping’s government has waged a repression campaign against hundreds of thousands of Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities. In 2020, the U.S. government blacklisted the firm for enabling human rights abuses.
Internal ICBC records describe how Lu Ping, the chief marketing officer of the ICBC subsidiary in New Zealand, “exhibited the outstanding qualities of a communist party member.” “Comrade Lu Ping” was nominated for a company-wide commendation in 2022 for his proactive role “fulfilling cash management needs” in New Zealand for Hikvision and Huawei, one of the bank’s most important clients.
China Capital also uncovered secret links between one of Austria’s most important aviation companies and a top Chinese producer of military aircraft. ICIJ’s partner in Vienna, profil, examined internal 2021 memos that discussed a $230 million loan to Future Advance Composite Components, which is affiliated with the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China.
While FACC, as the firm is known, publicly states that it produces aircraft parts exclusively for the civilian market, its Chinese owner has an “absolute leading position” in China’s defense industry and is the “sole manufacturer of all kinds of military aircraft and airborne equipment” in the country, according to the records.
ICBC bankers also discussed the possibility that the U.S. government could sanction AVIC in the future due to its links to China’s military apparatus. Though some London officers opposed extending the loans due to risk management concerns, they left the ultimate decision to ICBC’s Beijing headquarters. The documents do not state whether the bank approved the loan. AVIC did not respond to inquiries from profil.
Strategic deals revealed across Australia, Ghana, Belgium, the UK and Sweden
As part of China Capital, reporters also examined hundreds of credit application forms and other records that partly explained why ICBC London would want to pursue a deal. The documents revealed the geopolitical nature of some loans.
In Australia, ICBC issued “loss-making or marginal loans” to some of the country’s biggest resources and infrastructure companies, including Rio Tinto, Fortescue and Glencore, as a way of starting long-term relationships that would help advance Beijing’s political goals, the Australian Financial Review found.
The documents show how in 2015, Andrew Forrest, the billionaire CEO of Fortescue, an iron ore miner, made an emergency trip to Beijing to meet with ICBC’s chairman and seek assistance after the company was forced to cancel a $2.5 billion bond issuance because of unattractive interest rates.
Fortescue was struggling financially, but ICBC’s Sydney branch implored the Beijing headquarters to approve the loan at rates close to 30% below those offered by bond investors in the U.S., AFR reported. An internal memo cited Fortescue’s “significant strategic importance for the Chinese steel industry.”
ICIJ media partners in Ghana found evidence of loans awarded for similarly strategic reasons.
Ghana Business News reported how ICBC continued to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to the Ghana Cocoa Board, a government entity that supports and controls the production of cocoa — an important commodity — even though the company lacked transparency and was on a watchlist of borrowers in financial distress.
According to internal records, China stood to benefit from financing the firm, also known as Cocobod, since Chinese trade companies were key buyers and the deal helped cement the political alliance between Beijing and Accra. ICBC’s Brussels branch also participated in the loan to Cocobod, De Tijd reported, suggesting that the overseas units often helped each other when the clients were considered strategic for the bank and the party-state.
ICBC acquired a key role in the China-Africa trade thanks to its 19.7% stake in South African banking giant Standard Bank, The Africa Report found. Chinese authorities have approved the two institutions as joint renminbi-clearing banks — an arrangement that is expected to ease transactions in the Chinese currency across 19 countries where Standard Bank

So far this tax season, the IRS has received more than 100 million income tax returns for 2022.
That means tens of millions of households have yet to file their returns. If yours is among them, here are some last-minute tax-filing tips to keep in mind as the Tuesday, April 18 deadline approaches.
Not everyone has to file on April 18: If you live in a federally declared disaster area, have a business there — or have relevant tax documents stored by businesses in that area — it’s likely the IRS has already extended the filing and payment deadlines for you. Here is where you can find the specific extension dates for each disaster area.
Thanks to many rounds of extreme weather in recent months, for instance, tax filers in most of California — which accounts for 10% to 15% of all federal filers — have already been granted an extension until Oct. 16 to file and to pay, according to an IRS spokesperson.
If you’re in the armed forces and are currently or were recently stationed in a combat zone, the filing and payment deadlines for your 2022 taxes are most likely extended by 180 days. But your specific extended filing and payment deadlines will depend on the day you leave (or left) the combat zone. This IRS publication offers more detail.
Lastly, if you made little to no money last year (typically less than $12,950 for single filers and $25,900 for married couples), you may not be required to file a return. But you may want to anyway if you think you are eligible for a refund thanks to, for instance, refundable tax credits such as the Earned Income Tax Credit. (Use this IRS tool to gauge whether you are required to file this year.) You also are likely eligible to use IRS Free File (intended for those with adjusted gross income of $73,000 or less) so it won’t cost you to submit a return.
Your paycheck may not be your only source of income: If you had one full-time job you may think that is the only income you made and have to report. But that’s not necessarily so.
Other potentially taxable and reportable income sources include:
- Interest on your savings
- Investment income (e.g., dividends and capital gains)
- Pay for part-time or seasonal work, or a side hustle
- Social Security benefits or distribution from a retirement account
- Income from a rental property you own
Organize your tax documents: By now you should have received every tax document that third parties are required to send you (your employer, bank, brokerage, etc.).
If you don’t recall receiving a hard copy of a tax form in the mail, check your email and your online accounts — a document may have been sent to you electronically.
Here are some of the tax forms you may have received:
- W-2 from your wage or salaried jobs
- 1099-B for capital gains and losses on your investments
- 1099-DIV from your brokerage or company where you own stock for dividends or other distributions from their investments
- 1099-INT for interest over $10 on your savings at a financial institution
- 1099-NEC from your clients, if you worked as a contractor
- 1099-K for payments for goods and services through third-party platforms like Venmo, CashApp or Etsy. The 1099-K is required if you made more than $20,000 in over 200 transactions during the year. (Next year the reporting threshold drops to $600.) But even if you didn’t get a 1099-K you still must report all the income that you made over third-party platforms in 2022.
- 1099-Rs for distributions over $10 that you received for a pension, annuity, retirement account, profit-sharing plan or insurance contract
- SSA-1099 or SSA-1042S for Social Security benefits received.
“Be aware that there’s no form for some taxable income, like proceeds from renting out your vacation property, meaning you’re responsible for reporting it on your own,” according to the Illinois CPA Society.
One very last-minute way to reduce your 2022 tax bill: If you’re eligible to make a tax-deductible contribution to an IRA and haven’t done so for last year, you have until April 18 to contribute up to $6,000 ($7,000 if you’re 50 or older). That will reduce your tax bill and augment your retirement savings.
Proofread your return before submitting it: Do this whether you’re using tax software or working with a professional tax preparer.
Little mistakes and oversights delay the processing of your return (and the issuance of your refund if you’re owed one). You want to avoid things like having a typo in your name, birth date, Social Security number or direct deposit number; choosing the wrong filing status (e.g., married vs single); making a simple math error; or leaving a required field blank.
What to do if you can’t file by April 18: If you’re not able to file by next Tuesday, fill out Form 4868 electronically or on paper and send it in by April 18. You will be granted an automatic six-month extension to file.
Note, however, that an extension to file is not an extension to pay. You will be charged interest (currently running at 7%) and a penalty on any amount you still owe for 2022 but haven’t paid by April 18.
So if you suspect you still owe tax — perhaps you had some income outside of your job for which tax wasn’t withheld or you had a big capital gain last year — approximate how much more you owe and send that money to the IRS by Tuesday.
You can choose to do so by mail, attaching a check to your extension request form. Make sure your envelope is postmarked no later than April 18.
Or the more efficient route is pay what you owe electronically at IRS.gov, said CPA Damien Martin, a tax partner at EY. If you do that, the IRS notes you will not have to file a Form 4868. “The IRS will automatically process an extension of time to file,” the agency notes in its instructions.
If you opt to electronically pay directly from your bank account, which is free, select “extension” and then “tax year 2022” when given the option.
You can also pay by credit or debit card, but you will be charged a processing fee. Doing so, though, may become much more costly than just a fee if you charge your tax payment but don’t pay your credit card bill off in full every month, since you likely pay a high interest rate on outstanding balances.
If you still owe income taxes to your state, remember that you may need to go through a similar exercise of filing for an extension and making a payment to your state’s revenue department, Martin said.
Use this interactive tax assistant for basic questions you may have: The IRS provides an “interactive tax assistant” that can help you answer more than 50 basic questions pertaining to your individual circumstance on income, deductions, credits and other technical questions.

articles.title_orig: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.title_zh: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.content_orig:
America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
Long-standing educational programs such as Fulbright, Boren, and the Critical Language Scholarship are all suspended. A leader-level deal could bring them back and protect the students who take part.
- Rosie LevineExecutive Director of the U.S.-China Education Trust
- Rush DoshiCFR ExpertC.V. Starr Senior Fellow for Asia Studies and Director of the China Strategy Initiative
Derk Bodde set out for Beijing in 1948 expecting to spend a quiet year translating an esoteric work of Chinese philosophy. Instead, as the first recipient of the newly created Fulbright fellowship in China, he found himself an eyewitness to the Chinese Communist Party’s takeover, and his account of what he saw became a rare firsthand record for policymakers, academics, and the American public. When China closed to foreign contact for the next quarter-century, Bodde’s expertise didn’t just remain useful: it was irreplaceable.
Bodde’s story is a clear example of the ways in which in-country research is a proven and often indispensable tool to strengthen American expertise of foreign countries—and not only with friendly nations. But as Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping prepare to meet tomorrow in Washington, DC, only around two thousand Americans are studying in China, down from fifteen thousand a decade ago, and the public and private ecosystem that once supported deep American study of China is collapsing precisely when it is needed most.
That decline is due both to funding cuts and legitimate concerns that students may face risks of arbitrary detention in China. Currently, two American academics have been designated as wrongfully detained after traveling to China for academic purposes, creating risks that must be addressed by Beijing. Such cases are rare—the vast majority of Americans who study in China do so without incident—but they are real, and their chilling effect reaches far beyond the individuals involved. At the upcoming summit, Presidents Trump and President Xi should elevate specific programs like Fulbright into leader-level deliverables, with President Xi’s high-profile support for them at the summit providing implicit assurances that participants will not face undue risks from China’s security services.
This approach has some precedent. Exchange programs sometimes receive broad protections from leaders. Indeed, even at the height of the Cold War, the United States established the International Research and Exchanges Board (IREX) in 1968 as a formalized, bilateral academic exchange mechanism, sending generations of American Sovietologists into the Soviet Union, even as the two countries remained locked in rivalry. IREX and its successors, including the Committee on Scholarly Communication with the People’s Republic of China, which managed similar style exchanges with China before diplomatic normalization, were established to lend U.S. government protection to academic exchanges deemed essential to the national interest.
By contrast, the China programs that built a generation of expertise are now defunct. The Fulbright Program has been suspended in China since 2020, partly over risks that participating students and researchers might be detained by China. Alongside Fulbright, less well-known but essential U.S. government–funded programs specifically designed to encourage greater foreign area expertise in government have been suspended to mainland China, including the Boren Awards, the Critical Language Scholarship, the National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI-Y), and more.
At home, the area studies infrastructure in U.S. universities that was built in the 1950s, including the National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and Foreign Language and Area Studies (FLAS) fellowships, has been gutted amid cuts at the Department of Education. In recent weeks, new unclear federal restrictions on higher education’s ties to China have pushed some universities to conclude that even nonsensitive academic engagement—undergraduate study abroad included—carries too much risk: the University of North Carolina is the latest institution to pull down its study abroad program.
Critics of travel to China argue that Taiwan offers a safer alternative for Mandarin language study, and that the extent of state surveillance makes the risk of visiting China not worth the potential benefits. But Taiwan’s educational opportunities, while excellent, cannot fully substitute for the loss of access to China’s economy, society, and culture.
America needs a much deeper supply of China experts to handle a fast-changing relationship. In closed-door meetings compiled for the U.S.-China Education Trust’s 2026 report, America’s China Talent Challenge, stakeholders across the U.S. government, business, and academia described how their sectors depend on American expertise to interpret China’s actions—from geopolitics and security, to trade and supply chains—and to keep the United States competitive. The working group concluded that China expertise must be considered a national resource.
As Trump and Xi meet in Washington, progress on people-to-people diplomacy may be less challenging than in other domains. But both sides can take steps to improve the situation.
First, the Trump administration should negotiate with Beijing to elevate specific programs, from named legacy programs—including the Fulbright, Boren, Critical Language Scholarship, and NSLI-Y—to new initiatives, into summit deliverables. President Xi’s endorsement of these programs would provide implicit protection for those students who participate in them. President Trump could privately push to formalize assurances that participants will face no risks from China’s security services. And to make that gesture credible, Beijing should release detained academics.
Second, in tandem with these negotiations, the United States should reverse cuts to funding programs, which are in many cases entirely unrelated to China. The area studies infrastructure built nearly eighty years ago, to include National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and FLAS fellowships, has been gutted and should be restored. Congress should also fund new programs, purpose-built for today’s U.S.-China relationship. Scrutiny of university ties to China is in some cases warranted, but it should be scoped so that nonsensitive academic engagement, such as undergraduate study abroad and language programs, are able to proceed with appropriate safeguards.
To some, these proposals may seem unrealistic. But they are rooted in history and pragmatism. Washington has long had educational programs in countries with competitors and adversaries. Those programs were often sustained by leader-level understandings that they would be insulated from competitive dynamics in the relationship. Improving mutual understanding is inherently valuable. For both Washington and Beijing, it also reduces the risk of miscalculation. If the next generation of policymakers has no China experience, both countries will suffer.
A United States that no longer trains people who can read Chinese primary sources, sit in Chinese classrooms, or track policy implementation on the ground is hardly more secure and is substantially less capable. Rebuilding China expertise is not an act of goodwill toward Beijing. It is a hard-nosed investment in the United States’ atrophying ability to understand and compete with its most consequential rival.
The United States and China have few bright spots in the bilateral relationship, and fewer still that could be elevated into summit deliverables. Naming and insulating a handful of exchange programs from political and security pressures is in fact one of the most straightforward areas for cooperation that exists between the two countries.

articles.title_orig: US open to extending China trade truce, or bigger deal, Bessent says after meeting with He
articles.title_zh: US open to extending China trade truce, or bigger deal, Bessent says after meeting with He
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is open to discussing shared risks with China in upcoming AI talks this weekend, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios.
Why it matters: The Trump administration has flatly rejected calls from industry to pace or slow down the development of AI, citing a fierce race against China.
Bessent's scheduled meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng could provide an opening for talks on U.S.-China AI safety cooperation.
"The United States remains the leader in AI. And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems. We expect our discussions to cover both open and closed weight models," Bessent said in a statement to Axios.
"Bessent and [United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer] are the point guys on China. So it makes sense the secretary is in this position," a senior administration official said.
Driving the news: There will be multi-hour meetings in New York City, focused on AI, trade, rare earths, and other economic issues, building on previous discussions held in cities around the world, sources familiar said.
The agenda will remain flexible to allow for substantive discussion across the range of relevant issues, sources added.
Possible working-level meetings will continue into Monday, sources said.
Catch up quick: Bessent has played a key role in the Trump administration's AI agenda.
He was among the few cabinet members who flanked President Trump during a G7 press conference in June, where top AI CEOs and the administration discussed a U.S.-led effort to coordinate global AI standards.
Bessent also helped cool Anthropic's relations with the administration following a fallout with the Pentagon and is viewed as a reasonable actor who is trusted by the private sector and critical infrastructure operators, sources familiar have previously told Axios.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick led high-profile AI discussions during the G20 summit in North Carolina earlier this month, while Bessent is taking the lead on talks with China.
The big picture: Bessent's meetings in New York come days before Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's summit in Washington on Sept. 24.
AI CEOs have been calling for U.S.-China coordination on safety standards.
"All parties should jointly promote the open and inclusive development of AI for good and for all," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said this week, while pushing back on U.S. AI companies' calls to slow down and warning against "fear-mongering."
The bottom line: While a major breakthrough in U.S.-China safety cooperation remains a tall order, Bessent's involvement signals room for engagement on AI between the competing countries.

articles.title_orig: In A.I. Race, U.S. Models Have the Edge, but China Has Other Advantages
articles.title_zh: In A.I. Race, U.S. Models Have the Edge, but China Has Other Advantages
articles.content_orig:
Trump insists the US ‘win AI’ over China — or else. The reality is even more stark
Unlike when the US went all out to beat Russia to the moon, Trump is both feeding China the means of production on AI, and using Xi Jinping as a bogeyman to eschew guardrails for the tech. That strategy, writes Andrew Feinberg, ties in to something a handful of billionaires sorely need
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Less than 24 hours after declaring that the U.S. is “leading China by alot” in the race to develop cutting-edge Artificial Intelligence models, President Donald Trump will roll out a literal red carpet for the man most invested in changing that.
The president is set to host Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife for a state visit on Wednesday and Thursday — Xi’s first since he made a similar trip during the Obama administration almost a decade ago.
It follows a state visit to Beijing by Trump in May, during which the president hailed the “special relationship” between the United States and China and said he’d had “extremely positive and productive talks” on a variety of topics.
Trump has spent his entire political career complaining about the Sino-American trade relationship and has kept the U.S. in an on again, off again trade war with Beijing while casting himself as a China hawk in all but important domains.
He’s repeatedly stressed the need for a laissez-faire approach to AI regulation dating back to when he signed his first set of artificial intelligence executive orders in July 2025. But in practice, Trump’s administration has made "whatever it takes" look more like something closer to "whatever the market will bear.”
Initially, Trump said America had started the AI race and would win it, that no foreign country would be allowed to beat the US, and that it was now official policy to do whatever it takes to lead the world in the field. He’s made that a familiar refrain on the stump in his social media output as he’s cast AI as the defining contest of the century and China as the rival to beat.
But late last year, the White House gave permission for Nvidia to sell its advanced H200 processors to approved Chinese buyers on the condition that the Treasury Department take a quarter of the profits. It was a similar arrangement to the one they’d put into place earlier in 2025 for the weaker H20 chips.
The administration also appears poised to extend a pause on heightened export controls that had drawn China’s ire, leading Beijing to cut off U.S. supplies of rare earth materials before a truce — set to expire next month — broke the stalemate.
Take a look at some of the guests who will be at this week’s state dinner honoring Xi.
According to a senior administration official, the guest list includes Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Jane Fraser, and Tim Cook.
With the exception of Frazier, the head of Citi, all of those big tech executives have significant business interests in China — and nearly all have allied themselves with the administration since Trump returned to power.
And Trump knows they need one thing above all — access to Chinese rare earths.
Without them, Apple and Google can’t build phones. Dell can’t build computers. Huang’s Nvidia can’t build the AI chips that Altman and Pichai need for their AI platforms.
And if those things can’t happen, none of those executives will be keeping the GOP coffers full.
So when Trump says he wants the U.S. to stay ahead in the AI race, he probably thinks he’s telling the truth.
But that lead could vanish if his administration continues to allow exports of key AI chips, made by Huang’’s Nvidia, and that will continue to happen as long as Trump’s contributors’ enterprises need the rare earths that Xi’s government has held hostage.
And for now that leaves Americans, and maybe the world, at risk of a rogue AI “incident” or incidents, all because the bottom line was placed before public safety.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko revealed during a speech to youth leaders in Minsk that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin regularly joke and argue over which of them qualifies as the ultimate dictator.
The Belarusian leader's comments at "Youth. Belarus. Future." Sept. 17 also underlines the close alignment between Moscow and Minsk with Lukashenko enjoying his position as Europe’s longest-serving head of state.
Lukashenko has ruled over Belarus unhindered since 1994, with Putin leading Russia since 2012, also serving as president between 2000 and 2008.
"You know what they say about me?" Lukashenko asked the audience during his Sept. 17 address, according to Novaya Gazeta.
TRUMP SAYS US HELPED SECURE RELEASE OF 5 PRISONERS IN BELARUS DEAL, THANKS LUKASHENKO
"[I am] the last dictator, the second-to-last dictator in Europe. Dictator, dictator. Vladimir Putin and I often joke and argue over which of us is more of a dictator.
"They say I’m the last dictator, the last dictator in Europe. Dictator — so be it. Well, Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin and I often argue, jokingly, about which of us is the bigger dictator."
Lukashenko, 72, a former Soviet collective farm manager, is also known to be Putin’s closest international partner and ally.
While Minsk has not committed ground troops to the war in Ukraine, it serves as a strategic staging ground for Moscow, with Russia relying on Belarus for military and strategic support in its ongoing war against Ukraine.
According to the Kyiv Post, Belarus specifically provides Russia with key weapons components and allows its forces to launch military strikes from Belarusian territory.
An August report by Ukrainska Pravda also highlighted a new railway construction capable of handling military trains in Belarus' Gomel Oblast near the Ukraine border.
RUSSIA’S STRIKES NEAR MOLDOVA RAISE ALARM OVER PUTIN’S PLANS FOR EUROPE’S EASTERN FLANK
The strength of the relationship between the two countries comes as Western officials increase pressure on Moscow and its allies and with the two leaders reported to be in frequent contact.
After meeting in Moscow Aug. 27, Lukashenko officially congratulated Putin Sept. 21 after the Russian election results.
He praised the "unprecedented turnout of millions of voters" and the majority secured by the United Russia party, calling it a proper response to "cynical attempts from the outside to discredit the campaign and sow discord."
Addressing the youth forum in Minsk on political succession in Belarus, Lukashenko insisted no one is prepared to take over power.
"Never believe those who say that Lukashenko is ‘clinging to power with blue-knuckled hands’," he told the audience.
"Good Lord, let them say it. I have had my fill of this power to the point where I could not possibly want any more of it.
"The only question is whether you are capable today of taking over the country and holding on to it," he added. "If you are, start tomorrow. To be frank, I cannot yet answer that question positively. Do not take offense.
"I became a dictator then because I stood up against the entire ‘civilized world.'"
Western nations maintain strict economic pressure on Minsk. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys recently reiterated the Baltic nation's firm stance.
"We do not see any reasons why our position on Belarus should soften as Belarus is not changing its behavior," Budrys said.
"On our side, we have to be very exact and continue what works, and that is the pressure on the regime."
Despite international sanctions, Lukashenko announced Sept. 11 that Belarus has begun selling potash, a primary export used in fertilizer, to the United States.

While Western nations maintain economic restrictions over human rights abuses, U.S. sanctions on Belarusian potash were lifted after recent political prisoner releases, though European Union sanctions remain active.

articles.title_orig: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose of drugs, including fentanyl, coroner says
articles.title_zh: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose of drugs, including fentanyl, coroner says
articles.content_orig:
“Heroes” and “Nashville” star Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled an accident caused by the toxic effects of multiple drugs, including fentanyl, officials said Tuesday.
The Greenville County Coroner’s Office attributed her cause of death to the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol and Quetiapine.
There were no signs of trauma that would have contributed to the death, the release added.
Panettiere, 36, died Aug. 16 at a South Carolina apartment complex where she had been staying. Authorities found her unresponsive after a report of a cardiac arrest.
She had been in rehab just weeks before, according to a coroner’s report obtained by The Associated Press.
The detailed report released to the AP said a senior deputy coroner investigating the death discovered blue pressed pills and a straw on a table at the Airbnb apartment where the actor had been staying. It tested positive for fentanyl, according to the report, which also noted that a white powdery substance was found in her suitcase in a sunglasses case.
When the investigator called Panettiere’s father, he said she planned to spend her birthday five days later in Greenville, then head to Ukraine to visit her daughter.
In a statement Wednesday in response to the release of Panettiere’s cause of death, her mother, Lesley Vogel, called her daughter a “fighter.”
“She proudly owned this badge and I respected her prowess,” Vogel said. “She was transparent with her addictions and her numerous rehab attempts show her resolve to live a healthy life. We are all responsible for our choices.”
She added: “The loss of Hayden is palpable; grief permeates the soul and it will live with those who loved her forever. Let us not dishonor the amazing talent, intellect and beauty of this young woman who left this Earth far too soon.”
The Greenville Police Department said there were no signs of foul play during the initial response and investigation. The investigation into her death remains active, the department said Tuesday.
The Drug Enforcement Administration was also investigating Panettiere’s death.
Bill Bodner, the former special agent in charge of the DEA’s Los Angeles Field Division, noted that the quantity of drugs found in Panettiere’s system remains unclear. But three of the drugs listed in her autopsy became common among drug abusers in the 1990s and remain widely used.
The cocktail’s street name, he said, is “the Holy Trinity.”
Bodner identified those drugs as an opiate, which in Panettiere’s case was fentanyl; a muscle relaxer, or Methocarbamol; and an anti-anxiety medication, or Alprazolam.
Quetiapine is an antipsychotic drug typically used to treat conditions such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. 4-ANPP, or 4-Anilinopiperidine, is a precursor chemical used in the illicit manufacture of fentanyl, Bodner said.
He described the precursor as a likely sign that the fentanyl found in her system was illegal. The drug cocktail, he added, is “incredibly dangerous.”
“When used in combination, there’s a synergism,” he said.
Vogel said that despite Panettiere’s public struggles with addiction, she has “never heard Hayden speak of Fentanyl.” One exception, she said, was when Panettiere “warned her brother of the dangers as well as orchestrating his rehabilitation,” adding that her daughter “would never have chosen” the drug.
Panettiere’s on-again, off-again boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, was at the apartment complex at the time of her death and showed authorities what a police report described as a “bag of medication” he said she was taking.
An attorney for Hickerson did not immediately respond Tuesday to a request for comment on Panettiere’s death.
Bodner, who probed the overdose deaths of Michael Jackson, Matthew Perry and other celebrities, has said investigators were likely attempting to reconstruct Panettiere’s final days.
“They will use forensics to exploit her telephone, try to re-create the last two or three days of her life from looking at text messages, looking at phone calls, looking at interaction with people on social media,” the 32-year veteran of the DEA’s field office in Los Angeles said.
“Once there’s a timeline of what she was doing before her death, it becomes easier to kind of find where that drug distribution took place that killed her,” Bodner added.
Panettiere’s relationship with Hickerson — an aspiring actor from South Carolina — appeared to have ended in 2020 amid allegations of domestic violence, but her mother told NBC News that they were still seeing each other when she died.
Panettiere detailed those allegations, along with her struggles with addiction and postpartum depression, in her recently released memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning.”
Hickerson pleaded no contest to a charge of injuring a spouse or girlfriend in 2019 in Los Angeles, and he was sentenced to four years of probation, court records show. Panettiere sought a restraining order against Hickerson in 2020, though the outcome is unclear.
In a statement in August, a lawyer for Hickerson reiterated that police found no signs of foul play in Panettiere’s death. The attorney, Sloan Ellis, added that the actor’s death remained under investigation.
“Out of respect for Hayden’s loved ones and the ongoing investigation, there will be no further comment at this time,” Ellis said at the time.
Panettiere began appearing in television commercials as a child. She landed a breakout role on the NBC sci-fi series “Heroes” and later earned two Golden Globe nominations for portraying an ambitious and volatile country musician in “Nashville.”
In her memoir, Panettiere wrote that her life began to spiral after she had a daughter with Ukrainian heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. She began drinking heavily to cope with postpartum depression and Klitschko’s distance, she wrote.
Panettiere checked into rehab and gave Klitschko custody of their child in 2018.
If you or someone you know is struggling with a drug or substance abuse problem, call these numbers for help: The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s national helpline is 1-800-662-HELP (1-800-662-4357); the National Drug Helpline is 1-844-289-0879; and the American Addiction Centers’ hotline is (866) 464-3073.

articles.title_orig: Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
articles.title_zh: Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
articles.content_orig:
Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
Trump lawyers say White House access is ‘a privilege, not a right’; CNN, Politico and MS Now to present case in court after president banned outlets from White House grounds
Trump administration calls banned journalists' White House access 'a privilege, not a right,' brands coverage a security risk
In a new legal filing in the case over a trio of new outlets barred entry to the White House, Trump administration lawyers repeatedly defended the president’s ban by saying journalists were not entitled to access to the building.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” the filing stated.
The filing went on to assert that the three outlets – by publishing sensitive or classified information obtained through its reporting – constituted a national security threat, giving the president the right to ax their credentials.
Trump banned the three outlets – CNN, MS Now, and Politico – last Friday in a snap decision announced via social media. He branded the three outlets “fake news” and threatened future bans against other outlets could follow.
Early the following week, the three publications filed a joint lawsuit asking a federal judge to restore their access, alleging that the action was an illegal act of retaliation that violated their First Amendment rights. A president, they argued in their complaint, can’t bar access to journalists based on reporting he doesn’t like.
Since then, Trump has found himself in an escalating tit-for-tat with the press, which has responded to the ban with measures of solidarity. Several outlets have declined to publish any images or video of the president so long as the three outlets are denied access to the White House. And the members of Trump’s standard TV pool – five channels, including CNN, who take turns traveling with the president, filming his daily activities, and distributing that footage – have ceased their duties.
Trump administration drafting up plans for 90-day embargo on diesel exports: report
The Trump administration is readying to launch a 90-day ban on diesel fuel exports from the United States, following mounting calls from his party to take action to bring down the fuel’s price ahead of the midterm elections, POLITICO reported Wednesday.
Several people with inside knowledge of the conversations told POLITICO (currently one of three outlets banned from the White House by Trump) that the plan has created a schism within pro- and anti-embargo camps in the administration. It’s also prompted furor from the oil and gas industry that has broadly supported the president.
One oil industry executive privy to the conversations told the outlet that Trump seemed intent on announcing a ban by the end of the week.
The price of fuel has weighed heavily on Republicans in the lead-up to the midterms, which will determine whether Trump’s party retains control of Congress for the second half of his term. Trump ran in 2024 in part on bringing down the price of gas, but the war he helped kick off between the US and Iran, and the closure of vital oil shipping arteries it prompted, has sent the cost of fuel skyrocketing.
Diesel, in particular, has become a sore spot. The fuel for everything from semi-trucks to tractors to heavy machinery, it has surged in price even more than standard gasoline, to more than $6.50 per gallon.
That’s prompted some Republicans, especially those representing farming-heavy states, to publicly call on the president to take drastic action to lower the price of diesel.
The pushback, POLITICO reports, is coming from oil and gas executives and administration officials who warn that the embargo could raise fuel prices in the long run.
Yesterday, Britain’s new prime minister Andy Burnham navigated his way through a first high-stakes meeting with DonaldTrump at the UN general assembly in New York. His aides were delighted with how the meeting went, as Trump praised the US-UK relationship and described Burnham as a “natural businessman”.
The anticipated sticking points – theChagos Islands, WestBank settlement sanctions and Ireland – appear not to have derailed the talks nor cast a shadow over the future relationship.
In today’s edition of The Latest podcast, Lucy Hough speaks to the our policy editor in London, Kiran Stacey. You can also watch on YouTube.
'I am the code': Trump reportedly clashed with White House ballroom architect after dismissing safety concerns
The Washington Post (paywall) reports today that James McCrery II, the first architect on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m White House ballroom project, resigned after repeatedly clashing with the president, who dismissed his warnings that design features Trump was insisting on violated building safety codes.
McCrery withdrew from the project last October after warning Trump that a preliminary design he wanted “did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures”, according to the Post’s report, which cites two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by the paper.
The sources said Trump brushed off the architect’s concerns, and argued that no building codes apply to White House construction. “I am the code,” Trump reportedly said.
The Post previously reported that they had also clashed over the size of the ballroom. One document obtained by the paper features an image of a planned data center overlaid on a map of Manhattan, with a note that appears to be poking fun at McCrery’s concerns. “James,” it reads. “And you think we are big.”
Another note made in Sharpie makes clear Trump’s preference for Corinthian-style columns.
When approached by the Post, McCrery didn’t say why he stepped down. A White House official said it was “factually false and totally inaccurate” to suggest he left the project over issues with the code, and said he was a “valued member of the initial design team.”
Discussions about the safety issues continued for months after McCrery’s departure, according to White House records reviewed by the Post.
It is not clear from those records whether the safety issues he identified have been resolved in more recent designs by Shalom Baranes Associates, the architecture firm that took over McCrery’s firm’s role in the project late last year.
The ballroom project is – unusually – being overseen by the Executive Residence, rather than the General Services Administration or National Park Service. The small office is exempt from rules that require federal agencies to solicit competitive bids and disclose details to the public, the Post previously reported. Typically, it’s responsible for routine repairs, entertainment expenses, and the purchase of furniture, art and other items for the executive mansion.
Rubio, in his press conference, also touched on the war in Iran at several points, including on the surprise negotiations that took place yesterday between Trump administration envoys and the Iran delegation.
“I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough,” Rubio said. “But at the same time I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation.”
Little detail has been shared about what was discussed at that meetings, though Rubio framed the conversation as a continuation of the earlier back-and-forth between the two sides.
Rubio also notably insisted that Trump would be able to see through his campaign in Iran acting on his authority alone, even if Republicans lose control of Congress in November and if Democrats were to oppose the continuation of US operations against the country.
Rubio also briefly addressed Trump’s meeting with Delcy Rodriguez, the interim Venezuelan president, who last night posed for a friendly photo with Trump at a Manhattan hotel only miles from where her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was incarcerated.
“It was a short meeting, but it was a very important meeting,” Rubio said.

articles.title_orig: Son of Israeli ambassador to US critically injured in West Bank ramming attack
articles.title_zh: Son of Israeli ambassador to US critically injured in West Bank ramming attack
articles.content_orig:
The son of Israeli Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter was critically injured in a ramming attack in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday afternoon, according to regional authorities, one day before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s scheduled speech at the United Nations.
Neria Leiter, a reserve soldier manning a checkpoint near the settlement of Beit Horon, was rushed to a hospital in Jerusalem, according to emergency response services.
“Neria needs a miracle,” Leiter said in a statement on social media. “I believe in the power of prayer, and I believe that when the people of Israel unite, miracles happen.”
The driver of the car, 29-year-old Mahmoud Muhammad Mahmoud Suleiman, a Palestinian from the nearby village of Beit Ur al-Tahta, was shot and killed at the scene of the attack, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
Hamas praised the attack in a statement Wednesday, describing it as a “natural response” to Israeli actions in the West Bank and Jerusalem. The militant group in the Gaza Strip called for increased resistance against Israel but did not claim responsibility for the attack.
Leiter’s elder son, 39-year-old Moshe Yedidya Leiter, was killed fighting in Gaza in November 2023 in the first weeks of the war triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel the month before.
The ramming attack occurred just days after a shooting in the West Bank on the eve of the Jewish high holiday of Yom Kippur. On Sunday morning, Netanel Shukrun, a father of six from the settlement of Alei Zahav, was shot and killed while bathing at a natural spring in the West Bank as part of the holiday customs. Shukrun’s 16-year-old son credited his father with saving his life when he shouted out a warning to take cover.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) arrested the suspected shooter at a hospital near the West Bank city of Ramallah, the military said Sunday. Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for the death penalty in the case under a new law applying capital punishment to terrorism and nationalistic murders.
After the shooting, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the IDF chief of staff, said: “The IDF is on high alert, deployed and prepared with soldiers reinforced across all sectors, including throughout the fast. Our mission is clear and ongoing — to thwart terrorism, act decisively against every threat, and protect the citizens of the State of Israel.”
Since October 7, 2023, Israel has carried out waves of widescale military operations in the West Bank intended to target what officials view as centers of terrorist activity. The operations have led to the displacement of tens of thousands of Palestinians across the territory and military raids into Palestinian villages.
“Terrorism currently in Judea and Samaria is at its lowest level in decades,” Defense Minister Israel Katz said in early September, using the biblical name for the West Bank, “and we will take all necessary steps to prevent terrorism from rearing its head again.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
articles.title_zh: Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
articles.content_orig:
Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
The EU Industry Commissioner warned that the EU will consider using punitive trade measures if Beijing does not rebalance the trade deficit, which costs the bloc thousands of jobs every week.
The European Union "urgently" needs to act quickly to rebalance its "unsustainable" trade relationship with China, Commission Executive Vice-President for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy, Stéphane Séjourné, told Euronews, stressing that significant job losses are at stake.
Recent customs data showed the gap between the bloc's imports from China and exports to China, the trade deficit, ran at more than €1 billion a day in July.
"This trade rebalancing is becoming existential for Europeans," Séjourné said on Euronews' interview programme The Europe Conversation.
"Today we're losing thousands of jobs every week," he noted, adding that the EU already lost 250,000 industrial jobs last year. These were particularly concentrated in energy-intensive sectors and automotive supply chains. "It's urgent that we act, and urgent that we rebalance."
The EU, meanwhile, began crucial negotiations with Beijing in June this year, and has set a looming October deadline for concrete, "credible" outcomes. This will culminate in a high-stakes visit by EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to Beijing on 8 and 9 October, where Brussels is hoping to secure commitments from China that it will curb exports to the EU.
"The European Commission has put forward a proposal to the Chinese side to discuss this sector by sector and look at how we can rebalance things," Séjourné said. "This imbalance isn't sustainable, not for China or for the EU."
However, so far, Beijing has been resisting calls from the Europeans, pushing back against calls for voluntary export curbs.
The EU Industry Commissioner said that negotiation and discussion will be "given a chance," but that the Commission has been clear on the consequences of talks not producing the results.
"Trade defence tools are on the table," he warned. "Today we need credibility in how we use these tools, and we won't hesitate to use them to rebalance things."
Tools currently on the table include anti-dumping duties and tariffs against unfair subsidies (in industries such as electric vehicles and solar panels).
But Brussels is walking a tightrope when it comes to defending the EU market, as Chinese retaliation could see the country restrict exports of rare earths, essential to several of the EU's key industries, including defence.
The EU will also be keeping its eye on talks between Washington and Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping is landing in the United States for a three-day summit with US President Donald Trump, which is set to cover issues ranging from trade to AI and rare earths.
The outcome of these talks between the two economic superpowers could directly affect Europe's economic interests, Séjourné explained.
"We need a constructive dialogue between China and the United States. As we saw last year, the trade escalation between Washington and Beijing on these issues could spark a trade war, one that could even affect the European economy."
Last year, an explosive tit-for-tat trade war saw the US and China hike tariffs on each other's goods to dizzying heights. At the peak of this battle, the US imposed 145% tariffs on Chinese imports, while Beijing's retaliatory duties reached 125%.
For Europe, a trade war between the US and China hits hard, as astronomical tariffs on China inevitably lead to the diversion of Chinese goods from the US to the EU.
On the agenda this week in the US will be the looming expiration of the trade truce, due to expire on 10 November.
"I hope this dialogue can be constructive, that an agreement can be reached, and that the situation can be stabilised," Séjourné concluded.

articles.title_orig: Former NASA chief sounds alarm on China's lunar "exploration" plans
articles.title_zh: Former NASA chief sounds alarm on China's lunar "exploration" plans
articles.content_orig:
In a forthcoming memoir, former US politician and NASA Administrator Bill Nelson offers a blistering assessment of China, saying the United States must do all it can to retain its leadership in space exploration.
“Beijing’s intended strategy is to dominate the high ground of the twenty-first century,” writes Nelson in Space Odyssey, a book to be published by Harper Horizon in January 2027.
A former Congressman and Senator from Florida, Nelson served as a mission specialist on a space shuttle flight in 1986 and later as NASA administrator from May 2021 to January 2025 under President Biden. The book largely focuses on his space policy work in Congress and his tenure as NASA’s leader.
Nelson recounts how in early 2023, NASA assisted the US military when a Chinese spy balloon began traversing the United States. With its experience in using balloons to map the stratosphere and model atmospheric currents, NASA provided information on how to shoot the balloon down without endangering anyone on the ground.
He argues that the balloon saga offered further affirmation that the United States was enmeshed in a high-stakes competition with China for the high ground.
“What many Americans first registered as a balloon violating our airspace was really a warning that the next great rivalry will not be fought on land or sea but the skies above us and even beyond our atmosphere,” he writes. “The episode was also a window into the new space race that is swiftly approaching its most urgent phase, with the stakes even higher than the Cold War contest.”
Nelson has long been wary of China as a threat to the United States, noting his concerns about technology theft from the West. Unlike his predecessor under a Democratic president—former astronaut Charlie Bolden, who served as NASA leader under President Obama—Nelson supported the Wolf Amendment, which strictly limits cooperation between NASA and China’s space program.

articles.title_orig: Trump invites Putin to G20 in Miami, Rubio says
articles.title_zh: Trump invites Putin to G20 in Miami, Rubio says
articles.content_orig:
The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The invitation, which marks a significant reversal by the Trump administration of Russia’s international isolation, was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference on the sidelines of the United Nations conference in New York.
“We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio said in a televised press conference following a meeting with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with [Trump] but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.”
The Kremlin has not yet responded publicly to the invitation, which is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and other European leaders who have recently accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks to disrupt logistics and spread political uncertainty among Kyiv’s allies.
Russia remains a member of the G20 but Putin has not attended a summit of the body since 2019. He did attend one session virtually in 2023. The December summit is set to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club.
Rubio framed the invitation by saying that Trump was willing to meet with “virtually anyone” and that “in order to solve problems, you have to meet with people you disagree with”. He said Trump remained open to meeting with Putin one-on-one in other forums, if “there’s a purpose behind the meeting”.
The G20 is a forum of the world’s largest economies and includes the European Union, China, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other major countries.
European officials were upset by a decision to invite Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of the group’s top economic officials in August and refused to pose in a “family photo” with him at the summit.
Zelenskyy had said earlier this month that he would be ready to travel to the summit and would meet with Putin if he attended.
“We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle in an interview. “It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That’s it.”
The invitation comes shortly before Zelenskyy is expected to address the United Nations on Wednesday, when he is likely to seek to galvanize public opinion to maintain pressure on Russia to end its war against Ukraine.
Rubio on Wednesday also indicated that he had spoken with Lavrov about the accusations of “hybrid attacks” in Europe, saying that one concern about the war was that “it could metastasize and spread into other places”.
Trump is currently seeking to negotiate a partial ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that would include attacks on Russian oil refineries in order to take pressure off global energy prices.
In particular, Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt attacks against Russian oil in order to reduce prices on diesel fuel, which have spiked to almost double their price last year in the United States before midterm elections for Congress.
Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the United Nations on Tuesday for a rare face-to-face discussion of measures to end the war. Zelenskyy called for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin to end the war, but the Kremlin has declined past attempts for direct meetings with Zelenskyy.
“President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I’m not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
Despite efforts to broker a ceasefire, however, Russia has continued to pummel Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities with drone and missile attacks. Kyiv hit a major Russian oil refinery over the weekend in its largest attack on Russia’s capital yet.
For the past two days, Kyiv has come under particularly severe attack from jet-powered Shahed drones – swifter and harder to intercept than their predecessors. As has been the case since mid-August, the drone attacks have come in the daytime as well as at night, disrupting ordinary life, schools and kindergartens.
On Wednesday morning an acrid stench of burning filled the city centre after multiple explosions, and the clear autumnal sky was clouded with plumes of black smoke.
A petrol station, warehouses, a business centre and a transport infrastructure building were hit, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. As of mid-morning, one person had died and eight had been injured. Explosions were seen near the capital’s main railway station.
Congress last week passed a sweeping sanctions bill against Russia that would also give Trump the authority to levy 100% tariffs against top purchasers of Russian energy exports, including China and India. Democrats, who mostly opposed the bill, said that it gave Trump too much power to levy tariffs and that they could be used against US allies as well.
In response to what has happened, the House foreign affairs committee posted on X: “Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill 5 days ago. Today Rubio makes clear the administration has no intention of isolating Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.”
Charlotte Higgins contributed reporting from Kyiv

articles.title_orig: Where a powerful nor’easter could hit hardest this weekend
articles.title_zh: Where a powerful nor’easter could hit hardest this weekend
articles.content_orig:
Nor'easter's heavy rain, strong winds a threat from NC to New England
Coastal flooding is already affecting parts of the mid-Atlantic as the powerful nor'easter slides up the East Coast into this weekend.
A nor'easter will bring coastal flooding, high surf, wind and rain to parts of the East Coast through the weekend, with impacts from North Carolina and the Virginia Tidewater, to the Jersey Shore and New England.
The nor'easter hasn't yet gained strength. But the pressure difference between low pressure off the East Coast and high pressure over eastern Canada is driving gusty winds along the Eastern Seaboard.
Some gusts are topping 40 mph along the coast from Delaware to the Virginia Tidewater.
And those persistent winds are piling water from the ocean and bays along parts of the coast.
Minor to moderate coastal flooding was reported from parts of the Jersey Shore to southeast Virginia during Wednesday morning's high tide.
Flooding was reported at one intersection in downtown Norfolk, Virginia, early Wednesday morning, according to local news.
Get More of Our News on Google
Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value.
Here's a general timeline of the storm and its impacts over the next several days.
- Through Thursday: Coastal flooding at high tide, gusty winds from New Jersey to northern Outer Banks of North Carolina
- Friday: Rain, possibly heavy, stronger winds, and coastal flooding arrive in parts of southeast New England, Long Island; coastal flooding at high tide, gusty winds continue from New Jersey to Virginia Tidewater, northern North Carolina.
- Saturday: Locally heavy rain, strong winds possible over much of coastal, southern New England. High tide coastal flooding from New England to at least parts of the mid-Atlantic coast once again. Some at least light bands of rain possible as far west as Hudson Valley, New Jersey.
- Sunday: Nor'easter weakens, but rain showers, some gusty winds could linger over much of New England, possibly the Hudson Valley.
The map below shows the severity of coastal flooding forecast at high tide through Friday night or early Saturday, color coded by severity.
The most significant coastal flooding will be from the southern New Jersey shore to the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina, including the Virginia Tidewater, as well as Chesapeake Bay and Delaware Bay.
This flooding will happen for multiple high tides, possibly five or more, into at least early this weekend in these areas.
Given this repeated battering from high surf, beach erosion is possible along stretches of these beaches.
At least minor coastal high tide flooding will also develop in parts of coastal New England by late Friday into the weekend.
We're expecting the heaviest rain to fall over coastal New England from Friday through the weekend.
This could lead to flash flooding, especially in urban areas, including the Boston metro.
It could also compound any coastal flooding at high tide in parts of southeast New England.
Much lighter rainfall accumulations are expected farther west, in the light green colors in the map below.
In the New York City metro, the heaviest rainfall is expected in eastern Long Island, with less rain farther west in the New Jersey suburbs.
The strongest winds with this nor'easter are expected this weekend from coastal and southeast New England to eastern Long Island, with some gusts over 50 mph possible, at times.
In these areas, some downed tree limbs and power outages are possible, including the Boston metro, Providence and Cape Cod.
Otherwise, occasional gusts from 40 to 50 mph are possible farther down the coast from the Jersey Shore to Delaware, and the Virginia Tidewater.
Here are some tips to keep in mind if you plan to travel to the Northeast into this weekend:
- Northeast major hub airports: Delays are most likely at Boston-Logan this weekend and are possible, at times, at NYC's three major airports through the weekend
- Roads: Some downed tree limbs, trees and flash flooding are possible in southeast and coastal New England, as well as eastern Long Island. Avoid coastal areas from northern North Carolina to southeast New England around any high tides into the weekend.
You might think it is too early for a nor’easter, but the criteria for a nor’easter are met more often than you would think.
A nor’easter simply means that the winds blow into an area from the northeast. For the Northeast, that usually means an area of low pressure is just off the coast, which brings the winds in this direction.
(More: What is a nor’easter?)
Most people usually think of snow and ice with nor’easters and that is because nor’easters do tend to occur more in the late fall and winter.
The most notable nor’easters tend to bring heavy snow because these lows move up along the Gulf Stream, tapping into the warm ocean. This warm, moist air then clashes with the cold air over the Northeast to create heavy snowfall. Fortunately, this one is occurring way earlier, so it is all rain this time.

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
articles.content_orig:
Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.
In a victim impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".
Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions".
Weinstein has already spent six years in prison while he has faced three trials in New York over rape and abuse allegations. He has a separate conviction for sex crimes in Los Angeles.
He was originally convicted and sentenced in the Miriam Haley case in 2020. But in 2024, New York's highest court overturned the conviction, ruling Weinstein did not get a fair trial. He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley.
The 2020 trial heard testimony from three women: Haley, actress Jessica Mann, and model Kaja Sokola.
Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006, and a jury found him guilty on that charge.
"I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she told the BBC of her decision to testify.
But in that same trial, the jury found him not guilty of assaulting Sokola. No verdict was reached on an additional charge of rape related to Mann.

articles.title_orig: Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
articles.title_zh: Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
articles.content_orig:
Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
Global South countries will be worst affected by the phenomenon sweeping the planet from June to February.
The record global heat caused by this year’s powerful “super El Nino” could cause nearly half a million excess deaths worldwide by early next year, according to a report (PDF) published by the global research collaboration, Climate Impact Lab, on Wednesday.
So what does the report reveal, how has climate change supercharged the effects of El Nino and should we all be really worried?
